prompt: In many cities, traffic congestion is getting worse. What are the causes of this problem, and what measures could be taken to solve it?
essay:
Traffic congestion has become a serious issue in many large cities around the world. This essay will discuss the main reasons for this problem and suggest some possible solutions.

The main cause of congestion is the growing number of private cars. As people become richer, more families can afford a car, and many prefer driving to using public transport because it is more convenient. In addition, cities have grown quickly, so people often live far from their workplaces and have to travel long distances every day. Poor public transport in some areas also makes the situation worse, because buses are slow and unreliable.

There are several measures that governments could take. Firstly, they should invest in public transport such as metro systems and dedicated bus lanes, which would encourage people to leave their cars at home. Secondly, a congestion charge, like the one in London, could reduce the number of cars entering the city centre at busy times. Finally, companies could allow employees to work from home some days, which would reduce the number of commuters.

Some people believe that building more roads is the best answer. However, new roads often attract even more drivers, so after a few years the traffic is just as bad as before. For this reason, I think it is better to reduce the number of cars than to make more space for them.

In conclusion, congestion is mainly caused by the rise in car ownership and urban growth. Better public transport, road charges and flexible working could help to solve the problem.

prompt: Some people believe that universities should focus only on academic studies, while others think universities should also prepare students for employment. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
essay:
Whether universities should confine themselves to scholarship or also equip students for the labour market is a long-standing debate. While I accept that academic depth remains the core purpose of higher education, I would argue that preparing graduates for employment is a legitimate and increasingly necessary complement to it.

Those who favour a purely academic focus contend that universities exist to advance knowledge rather than to serve as training centres for employers. On this view, disciplines such as philosophy or pure mathematics cultivate rigorous thinking whose value cannot be measured by immediate job prospects, and an institution preoccupied with employability risks diluting intellectual standards in pursuit of short-term market demands.

Proponents of a broader mission, however, point out that most students now enrol precisely because a degree is expected to improve their career prospects, often at considerable personal cost. If graduates leave without practical competencies such as communication, teamwork or familiarity with professional tools, universities arguably fail the very people who fund them. Moreover, structured internships and applied projects can deepen rather than undermine academic understanding, since theory is frequently clarified when it is tested against real problems.

In my view, the two aims are not mutually exclusive. A well-designed curriculum can preserve demanding academic content while embedding opportunities to apply it, so that students graduate both intellectually capable and employable. In conclusion, although scholarship should remain the foundation of higher education, universities that ignore employment preparation are neglecting a responsibility they now clearly share. Ultimately, the most valuable graduates will be those who can both think deeply and act effectively, and universities are uniquely placed to develop both.
